extracted.intended_audience: college/university students (composition or research classes) preparing annotated bibliographies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing single annotated bibliography entries (MLA or APA): provide a correctly formatted citation plus a concise summary, critical analysis, and statement of the work's usefulness for the writer's project or teaching. Examples illustrate structure and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct bibliographic citation (MLA or APA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin the annotation with a properly formatted bibliographic citation in the required style (examples shown in MLA and APA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MLA example: 'Lamott, Anne. Bird by Bird: Some Instructions on Writing and Life. New York: Anchor Books, 1995. Print.' APA example: 'Ehrenreich, B. (2001). Nickel and dimed: On (not) getting by in America. New York: Henry Holt and Company.' Include author name(s), year (APA), title formatting, publication place and publisher, and medium if required (e.g., 'Print' for MLA). Follow the punctuation and ordering conventions of the chosen style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of work
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a concise, objective summary of the source's content and main claims (no evaluation in this part).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize the author's purpose, approach, major topics, and scope in a few sentences. Examples: describe the book's honest/advice-driven tone and topics (plot development, perfectionism, writing exercises) or the journalist's experiential research methods and jobs undertaken. Keep to essential information so the reader understands what the work is about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of work (critical evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer a critical appraisal of the source: its strengths, weaknesses, methods, credibility, and overall contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the author's perspective, reliability, methods, and limitations (e.g., acknowledgement of experimental limits and ethical implications). Note whether the work is well-researched, timely, descriptive, or simply anecdotal. Mention style, tone, and usefulness (e.g., 'sane advice', 'down-to-earth humor', 'indispensable because of its honest perspective'). You may comment on appropriateness for your needs or curricular inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility / relevance to your project or teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly state how you will use the source in your own project, research, or classroom (what it contributes and how it will be applied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific: identify chapters, exercises, statistics, or expert citations you will draw on and explain how they will support your work (e.g., generate class discussion, provide drafting exercises, contextualize personal experience, supply logos or ethos). Example phrasing: 'I will use Ehrenreich’s statistics and citation of noted experts to problematize my own situation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Include labeled structural sections (SUMMARY, ANALYSIS, UTILITY)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize the annotation into clear labeled sections corresponding to summary, analysis, and utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use headings (as in the samples: <SUMMARY of WORK>, <ANALYSIS of WORK>, <UTILITY of WORK>) and keep each section focused and concise (a few sentences to a short paragraph). This structure signals to the reader the distinct purposes of each part of the annotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss methodological and ethical considerations when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: When the source uses research methods or experiential approaches, evaluate their rigor and ethical implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the author's awareness of methodological limits and any ethical issues (for example, Ehrenreich's experiential research and its limitations). Indicate whether the author is transparent about methods and whether supplementary scholarly research supports the work. This assessment belongs under Analysis but is particularly important for empirical or investigative sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify specific types of evidence or rhetorical appeals to be used
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify which elements of the source (statistics, anecdotes, expert citations, exercises, tone) you will leverage in your own argument or teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name the rhetorical resources (logos—statistics; ethos—expert citations; pathos—anecdotes/humor) and explain how each will function in your work. The sample shows using statistics (logos) and citations of noted experts (ethos) to support an argument about minimum wage and personal context.
